item.title: Do Programmable Thermostats Actually Cut Heating Bills?
item.description:
Quick Answer

Yes — but only if you actually program it. Department of Energy guidance says a setback of 7–10°F for 8 hours a day (asleep or away) can save up to 10% per year on heating and cooling. The catch: the savings come from the schedule you set, not the hardware. Energy Star stopped certifying programmable thermostats in 2009 largely because so many owners never changed the factory defaults — and those households often saw little to no savings.

item.title: How to Lower Your Electric Bill: The Complete Guide (2026)
item.description:
Quick Answer

You can cut your electric bill 20–40% with the highest-ROI moves: raise summer AC to 78°F (or drop winter heat to 68°F) saving $100–$300/year, switch to LEDs ($75/year), lower the water heater to 120°F ($40–$80/year), seal air leaks ($60–$200/year), shift laundry and dishwashing to off-peak hours, and kill vampire loads with smart strips ($50–$180/year).

  • Heating and cooling drive 40–50% of home energy costs — start there.
  • Most utilities run a free home energy audit; call before you spend a dollar.

Your electric bill is too high. You’ve tried turning off lights, but it barely made a dent. You want real savings—$50, $100, even $150 per month—and you want to know exactly what to do and what it’ll cost.

item.title: Understanding kWh Usage: What Uses the Most Electricity in Your Home
item.description:
Quick Answer

A kilowatt-hour (kWh) measures how much electricity you use over time — one kWh equals using 1,000 watts for one hour. The average U.S. household uses about 886 kWh per month, costing roughly $115-150 depending on local rates.

  • A 100-watt light bulb running for 10 hours uses 1 kWh
  • Your HVAC system typically accounts for 40-50% of total usage
  • Monitor your usage daily to spot unusual consumption patterns

For more detail, see How to Read Your Electric Bill.
